claims.text: The equilibrium price of a market is the price at which the quantity consumers are willing and able to buy equals the quantity sellers are willing and able to offer, so the market clears; a price change is a move from one equilibrium price to a new one.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The causes of price changes are changes in market conditions: a change in a condition of demand, such as consumers' incomes, the prices of related goods, tastes or the number of consumers, shifts the demand curve, and a change in a condition of supply, such as input costs, technology, the number of sellers or the weather, shifts the supply curve.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A price change runs from a shift to the price, not the other way round: a change in a market condition shifts a whole curve and this causes the equilibrium price to change, whereas a change in the good's own price shows as a movement along unchanged curves and is itself part of the consequence; the test is which side moved first - a condition outside the price, or the price itself.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: When floods destroyed the vegetable gardens around Oshakati, a condition of supply changed, the supply curve shifted left, and the price of a bag of vegetables at the weekend market rose from N$20 to N$26: the cause of the price rise was the weather, and the price rise was its consequence.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: With supply unchanged, a rightward shift of demand tends to raise both the equilibrium price and the quantity sold, so consumers pay more per unit while sellers usually sell more; a leftward shift of demand tends to lower both.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: With demand unchanged, a rightward shift of supply tends to lower the equilibrium price and raise the quantity sold, while a leftward shift tends to raise the price and lower the quantity sold, so the same shift usually helps one side of the market while it squeezes the other.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The consequences of a price change for a market are read as a pair: the new equilibrium price, and the new equilibrium quantity - the quantity actually bought and sold at the equilibrium price over a period of time, which is the market's sales.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A demand-and-supply diagram shows the consequences of a changed market condition in a form that can be read in words: label price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis, draw and label the original demand and supply curves, shift the curve whose condition changed in the correct direction, mark the new crossing as the new equilibrium, and state in words what the diagram shows - the new price and the new quantity sold against the old.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.
